title: Pulses Work Where Steady Signals Fail

scenes.tts: Can a steady signal fail where pulses work? Gonadotropin releasing hormone, G n R H, is a peptide from the hypothalamus. It tells the pituitary to release the gonadotropins, which drive the ovaries and testes. In 1978, Belchetz and colleagues studied rhesus monkeys whose hypothalamic lesions had abolished gonadotropin release.
scenes.caption: Can a steady signal fail where pulses work? Gonadotropin-releasing hormone, GnRH, is a peptide from the hypothalamus. scenes.visual: A steady bar and a pulse train face a question mark. Then a chain builds: hypothalamus, GnRH arrow, pituitary, gonadotropin arrow, ovaries and testes. A name label appears for Belchetz and colleagues, 1978; the hypothalamus is marked as lesioned and the gonadotropin arrow turns dashed.
scenes.narration: Can a steady signal fail where pulses work? Gonadotropin-releasing hormone, GnRH, is a peptide from the hypothalamus. It tells the pituitary to release the gonadotropins, which drive the ovaries and testes. scenes.tts: They gave G n R H continuously, or once an hour. Hourly pulses restored gonadotropin secretion. A constant infusion did not. Clinics use the same effect on purpose, keeping a G n R H agonist present to shut gonadotropin output down.
scenes.caption: They gave GnRH continuously, or once an hour. Hourly pulses restored gonadotropin secretion. A constant infusion did not. Clinics use the same effect on purpose, keeping a GnRH agonist present to shut gonadotropin output down.
scenes.visual: Two stacked timelines: a flat yellow line labelled continuous, and yellow spikes an hour apart. Result chips: pulses restored (green), constant not restored (grey). Then both clear and a clinic panel shows a GnRH agonist kept present leading to gonadotropin output shut down.
scenes.narration: They gave GnRH continuously, or once an hour. Hourly pulses restored gonadotropin secretion. A constant infusion did not. Clinics use the same effect on purpose, keeping a GnRH agonist present to shut gonadotropin output down.

scenes.tts: One general possibility is that off switches build up while a signal is on, and need a gap to reverse. Pulses give that gap. But a kinase mark and an arrestin cannot be the whole explanation. Willars and colleagues showed in 1999 that the mammalian G n R H receptor has no C terminal tail. So it resists phosphorylation by agonist, and resists rapid desensitization.

scenes.visual: Two columns, constant signal and pulses, each with a yellow signal strip and a red off-switch trace: it climbs under the constant signal and falls back in the gaps. Then a receptor bar in a membrane with its tail end bare, labelled no C-terminal tail, with chips for resists phosphorylation and resists rapid desensitization.

scenes.tts: A failure at the receptor would show as fewer receptors on the surface, or less second messenger made per dose. A failure downstream would leave the receptor's own output normal, while hormone release falls. Measure second messenger output, and you can tell the two apart. Published work answers only part of this question.
